title: My Ex Humiliated Me at the Mall, Then a Stranger Wrapped His Arm Around My Waist and Called Me Babe. When I Learned Who He Really Was, Everything Changed
fb_text:
My Ex Humiliated Me in Front of Everyone at the Mall. Then a Stranger Put His Arm Around My Waist and Called Me "Babe." My Ex Hurried Away in Fear. But When I Found Out Who That Man Really Was, Everything Changed...

"Does your new boyfriend know you live above a laundromat, or are you still pretending you're going somewhere in life?"

My ex made sure his voice carried far enough for everyone near the coffee counter to hear.

Then he laughed.

I was thirty years old, wearing a worn green florist's apron and holding a six-dollar coffee. I was facing the man who had spent three years convincing me I would never accomplish anything worthwhile.

My name is Josie Alder.

Until that Monday afternoon, I'd believed the most embarrassing moment of my life was the day Miles Dempsey walked out of our apartment and told me I wasn't worth waiting for.

I was wrong.

"Seriously, Josie." Miles looked me over from head to toe. "The same apron? The same job? I thought you'd have figured things out by now."

Two women waiting for their drinks turned to stare.

I tightened my grip on the paper cup.

"I'm working, Miles."

"Clearly."

He gestured toward the little flower kiosk across the hallway.

Petal Line.

It was a sixty-eight-square-foot space full of chilled roses, cheap ribbon and a tiny counter. For five years I had built arrangements there for weddings, birthdays, anniversaries and funerals.

Miles had always called it my little vegetable stand.

Now he stood in front of me in a perfectly fitted navy jacket and expensive shoes, wearing a watch that probably cost three months of my rent.

"I heard you got promoted," I said, hoping to change the subject.

His grin widened.

"Senior leasing consultant. Brightwell Retail Partners. We handle some of the biggest commercial properties around Charlotte."

"Congratulations."

"Thanks. You know the difference between us, Josie?"

I said nothing.

"I finally stopped being afraid of success."

He stepped closer.

"And you never stopped being comfortable with failure."

My chest tightened painfully.

I wanted to tell him about the wedding contract I'd landed last month. I wanted to tell him about the fourteen-hour days, and the online courses I took after every shift.

Instead, I kept staring at my coffee.

Miles knew exactly how to get to me. He knew anger made it hard for me to find the right words. He knew my first instinct was silence.

And he knew my silence made him feel in control.

"Tell you what."

He opened his wallet and pulled out a fifty-dollar bill.

Then he pushed it into the front pocket of my apron.

"Buy yourself something nice. Maybe a real outfit."

I took the money out immediately.

"Take it back."

"Oh, come on. Don't be dramatic."

"I'm serious."

He chuckled again.

"Still too proud to accept help, huh? That's why you'll always..."

Suddenly, a man's hand rested gently against my waist.

"Babe," a deep voice murmured beside me, "I've been looking everywhere for you."

I froze.

The stranger next to me was tall and broad-shouldered. He wore a charcoal overcoat over a white shirt, the sleeves neatly folded beneath his cuffs.

He looked about thirty-six, with dark hair and calm gray eyes. He was handsome enough for the cover of a business magazine.

And I had absolutely no idea who he was.

His eyes dropped to the fifty-dollar bill in my hand.

Then he turned to Miles.

"Is this gentleman bothering you?"

Miles opened his mouth.

Nothing came out.

It was astonishing. The man who'd just spent five minutes publicly tearing me down suddenly looked as if the floor had disappeared under his feet.

His eyes went wide.

"Mr. Vale?"

The stranger barely reacted.

"Do we know each other?"

Miles swallowed hard.

"I'm Miles Dempsey. Brightwell Retail Partners. We met at the redevelopment presentation last month."

"Ah."

The man gave a slight nod.

"Then you understand the importance of professional conduct."

All the color drained from Miles's face.

"I wasn't... I mean, Josie and I used to date."

"That explains the familiarity."

The stranger kept his hand resting lightly at my waist.

"It doesn't explain the disrespect."

For the first time in three years, I watched Miles lose an argument before he had even tried to defend himself.

"Right. Absolutely. Sorry."

He glanced at me, and for once he looked truly frightened.

"Good seeing you, Josie."

Then he hurried off, so fast that he nearly crashed into a woman pushing a baby stroller.

I watched him disappear.

The stranger took his hand away at once.

"Sorry about that," he said. "I should have asked before touching you. He looked like he wasn't going to stop."

I turned to face him.

"Who are you?"

"Elliot Vale."

"Am I supposed to recognize that name?"

He seemed genuinely amused.

"No. That's actually refreshing."

I looked down the corridor where Miles had vanished.

"Why did he look like he'd seen a ghost?"

"Probably because he expected you to stay silent."

That didn't satisfy me.

"That's not the whole reason."

"No," Elliot admitted. "Probably not."

I held out the fifty-dollar bill.

"Here. Since you're apparently important enough to terrify my ex, you can give this back to him."

He studied the money, then looked at me.

"I wouldn't know where to find him."

"Lucky you."

He burst out laughing.

It wasn't the polished laugh people use to make a good impression. It was real.

Then his phone vibrated.

He checked the screen, and his smile vanished.

"Actually," he said, "I have a rather embarrassing problem."

"Does it involve another man insulting someone near a coffee machine?"

"Unfortunately, it's worse."

"How much worse?"

"My mother."

I blinked at him.

He slid the phone into his coat pocket.

"My mother has invited a woman to dinner tonight, someone she thinks I should marry."

"Congratulations?"

"I've met her twice."

"Sounds promising."

"My mother has already discussed wedding venues."

I stared at him.

He went on, with surprising seriousness.

"And I just told her I'm bringing my girlfriend."

I slowly glanced over my shoulder.

Then I looked back at him.

"No."

"I haven't asked anything yet."

"You're about to."

"Would you consider coming to dinner with me?"

I laughed.

Then I stopped, because I realized he was completely serious.

"You want me to pretend to be your girlfriend?"

"For one evening."

"You don't even know my last name."

"Alder," he said, glancing at the embroidered badge on my apron.

I quickly covered it with my hand.

"That's cheating."

"I'm willing to learn the rest."

I should have said no and walked away. Any sensible woman probably would have.

But I kept seeing Miles standing in front of me, smirking while strangers listened to him describe my life as a failure.

I remembered three years of being told no accomplished man would ever choose someone like me.

And I couldn't forget how scared Miles had looked when Elliot put his arm around my waist.

"What exactly happens at this dinner?" I asked.

"My mother tries to control my future. My father pretends not to notice. My younger sister makes everything worse. And a perfectly respectable woman named Audrey Beckett sits there while everyone discusses our hypothetical children."

"Sounds delightful."

"It isn't."

"And afterward?"

"We shake hands, thank each other, and never have to do this again."

I studied his face.

"Are you dangerous?"

"Only to poorly managed construction budgets."

"What does that mean?"

"I build things."

It was possibly the vaguest answer I'd ever been given.

I looked toward my flower stand. My manager was busy arguing with a delivery driver.

"My shift ends at seven."

"I can pick you up at seven-fifteen."

"One dinner," I insisted.

"One dinner."

"No kissing. No ridiculous stories about romantic vacations. And absolutely no pretending we're engaged."

"Agreed."

I held out my hand.

He shook it.

Just then, his phone buzzed again.

This time, I could see the screen.

The message came from a contact saved as Mother.

Audrey's parents are coming tonight. Please don't embarrass this family again. I expect you to arrive alone.

Elliot read it.

Then he looked up at me.

A flicker of determination crossed his face.

"Well," he murmured, "this should be interesting."

I had no way of knowing that agreeing to one pretend date would pull me into a family capable of changing my entire future.

And I certainly didn't realize that the man who had defended me was tied to the very company secretly preparing to destroy my livelihood.

I wouldn't find that out until later.

By then, pretending to be in love with Elliot Vale would be the least dangerous deception between us...

I'm Josie Alder. I was thirty, wearing a worn green florist's apron and holding a six-dollar coffee. In front of me stood Miles Dempsey, the man who had spent three years convincing me I'd never amount to anything.

The Humiliation

"The same apron? The same job?" Miles said, looking me over. "I thought you'd have figured things out by now."

Across the hallway was Petal Line, my sixty-eight-square-foot flower kiosk. I had spent five years there making arrangements for weddings, birthdays and funerals. Miles used to call it my little vegetable stand. Now he was a senior leasing consultant at Brightwell Retail Partners, and he told me he had "finally stopped being afraid of success."

I wanted to tell him about the wedding contract I'd just won, the fourteen-hour days and the evening courses. Instead I stared at my coffee, as I always had. When he tucked a fifty-dollar bill into my apron pocket and told me to buy "a real outfit," I took it out and told him to take it back.

The Stranger

Then a hand settled gently at my waist.

"Babe, I've been looking everywhere for you."

The man beside me was tall, in a charcoal overcoat, with calm gray eyes. I had never seen him before. Miles recognized him instantly. "Mr. Vale?" he stammered, and the color drained from his face. A few polite words about professional conduct later, Miles mumbled an apology and hurried away.

The stranger let go at once and apologized for touching me without asking. His name was Elliot Vale, and he built things. Then his phone buzzed. His mother had invited a woman to dinner, someone she hoped he'd marry, and he had already told her he was bringing a girlfriend.

I said no. Then I remembered Miles smirking and the years of being told no accomplished man would choose me. We agreed on one dinner, with no kissing and no pretend engagement.

The Dinner

Elliot's mother was exactly as controlling as promised. His father stayed quiet. His sister made things worse. Audrey Beckett and her parents sat politely while everyone discussed a future that nobody had asked about.

When his mother questioned my work, I didn't go silent. I told her about Petal Line, the five years of early mornings and the wedding contract I'd earned myself. For once, the words came easily.

Audrey caught my eye across the table and smiled. Later, in the hallway, she admitted she had no wish to marry anyone her mother had chosen either. Elliot's father quietly told me it was the first honest conversation his family had had in months.

The Truth

Elliot walked me to my door afterward. He said he wanted to tell me something before I heard it elsewhere. His company was part of the mall redevelopment, and Miles's employer, Brightwell, was handling the leasing. Elliot had noticed that Brightwell's plans quietly pushed out the smallest tenants, including Petal Line, with almost no notice.

That was why Miles had panicked. He knew Elliot could uncover exactly what he'd been hiding.

I was furious, and I told him so. I had agreed to one pretend dinner, not to being used as a way into a problem I didn't know existed. Elliot didn't argue. He said I had every right to be angry, and that he'd rather lose my trust honestly than keep it through silence.

The Ending

He kept his word. Within weeks, Elliot demanded a full review of the leasing plans. The notices to small tenants were reissued with fair terms, and Petal Line kept its place in the hallway. Miles was removed from the project. I never heard him laugh at me again.

My business grew. The wedding contract led to others, and eventually I hired my first assistant.

As for Elliot, we started over with no pretending. He came to the kiosk on Mondays and bought one rose at a time, and he learned the rest of me slowly, just as he'd promised.

I had gone into that dinner to prove I wasn't a failure. What I really learned was that I'd never been one. I had only been standing next to someone who needed me to believe it.
